papers.title: Bolek: A Multimodal Language Model for Molecular Reasoning
papers.abstract: Molecular property models increasingly support high-stakes drug-discovery decisions, but their outputs are often difficult to audit: classical predictors return scores without rationale, while language models can produce fluent explanations weakly grounded in the input molecule. We introduce Bolek, a compact multimodal language model that grounds natural-language reasoning in molecular structure by injecting a Morgan fingerprint embedding into an instruction-tuned text decoder. Bolek is fine-tuned on molecular alignment tasks, including molecule description, RDKit descriptor prediction, and substructure detection, and on downstream reasoning over 15 TDC binary classification tasks using synthetic chains-of-thought anchored in concrete molecular features. Across these tasks, Bolek outperforms its Qwen3-4B-Instruct base on all endpoints in yes/no mode and on 13 of 15 in chain-of-thought mode, raising mean ROC/PR AUC from 0.55 to 0.76. It also outperforms TxGemma-9B-Chat on 13 of 15 binary classification tasks despite being less than half its size. Bolek's explanations are more grounded than those of the baseline LLMs: it cites numerical descriptors 10-100x more often per chain-of-thought, and the cited values agree strongly with RDKit for key descriptors such as TPSA, MolLogP, and MolWt (Spearman rho = 0.87-0.91). Generalisation extends beyond the training panel: on 15 unseen TDC classification endpoints, Bolek matches TxGemma on five, and it produces non-trivial rank correlations on three held-out regression endpoints despite never seeing downstream regression during training. These results suggest that targeted modality injection and reasoning supervision tied to verifiable molecular features can yield compact, auditable molecular reasoning models.

papers.title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
papers.abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), an extension of quantum selected configuration interaction (QSCI), is a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for molecular ground-state energies. By replacing variational optimization with quantum sampling, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and directly reconstructs correlated wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery mainly enforces symmetry constraints without targeting the most physically relevant configurations, often yielding oversized subspaces and costly classical diagonalization. We introduce QSCI-RBM, a compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and integrate it within Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET). The RBM learns the distribution of dominant determinants from hardware samples, generating high-probability configurations. Sampling was performed on IBM Heron R1 (\texttt{ibm\_torino}) for CH$_5$NO, R2 (\texttt{ibm\_fez}) for C$_2$H$_4$, and R3 (\texttt{ibm\_boston}) for the larger H$_2$O benchmark and the protein-ligand system. After validating on these benchmarks of increasing active-space size, we simulate the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (M\textsuperscript{pro}), fragmented into ten DMET impurities. Both DMET-QSCI-RBM and a DMET-SQD baseline reach chemical-potential self-consistency within four $\mu$-iterations. At the converged chemical potential, DMET-QSCI-RBM lies within $0.05\,\mathrm{mHa}$ of DMET-FCI while accessing on average only $0.22\%$ of the symmetry-preserving configuration space, versus $0.55\,\mathrm{mHa}$ at $33.0\%$ for DMET-SQD, leading to a $\sim$153-fold subspace reduction. RBM-assisted expansion thus yields far more compact hardware-derived determinant spaces at equal or better accuracy, reducing classical overhead for scalable quantum embedding of biological systems on real hardware.

papers.title: PeptSol: A Translational Benchmark for Protected-Peptide Solubility in Drug Manufacturing
papers.abstract: Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) offers a scalable route to peptide manufacturing, but route development still depends on empirical solvent screens because each protected intermediate must be soluble for reaction and recoverable for purification. The protecting groups, terminal modifications, and noncanonical residues that govern this behaviour are poorly represented in existing peptide property benchmarks, limiting the ability to develop and rigorously evaluate molecular representation models for LPPS-relevant prediction tasks. We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell. No foundation model consistently outperforms a baseline combining chemical fingerprints with explicit molecular descriptors, and model rankings vary across prediction tasks and data splits. The dataset, evaluation protocol, and baselines establish a standard for measuring progress on molecular representations for synthesis-aware peptide developability.

papers.title: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets
papers.abstract: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context. Using an intersection-over-union objective and evaluation metric (range-IoU), RangeFinder achieves a range-IoU of $0.464 \pm 0.002$, outperforming all deployable baselines while requiring only $12.2$ ms per pocket. We also quantify our method's ability to reduce the ligand search space while retaining compatible binders; in this regard, RangeFinder achieves a Reduction-Recall F-Score of $0.543 \pm 0.011$ --- once again outperforming all deployable baselines. Ablation experiments indicate that RangeFinder's performance depends more strongly on the density and quality of ligand supervision than on any individual input modality or specialized training strategy. Together, these results position RangeFinder as an inexpensive and effective molecular filtering prior, with demonstrated potential in narrowing the ligand search space of target pockets before docking, generation, or synthesis. The code for this project can be found at: https://github.com/alannadels/RangeFinder.

papers.title: Canonic hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium: Reassessing the role of cooperativity
papers.abstract: Hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium is normally studied within the grand canonical ensemble, which assumes that each hemoglobin is immersed in a reservoir of unbound oxygen molecules of the plasma. We show that this assumption is incorrect inside the RBC (red blood cell or erythrocyte), where the hemoglobin concentration is larger than the concentration of unbound oxygen in plasma. We suggest a better model, where a single hemoglobin and a few oxygen molecules around it reach a canonical equilibrium at a fixed volume (determined from the RBC structure) and a fixed temperature. The basic models of hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium -- Pauling's model and Monod-Wyman-Changeux model -- can be reformulated for this canonical situation. They predict cooperative interaction energies, which are significantly lower than predictions of the same models in the grand canonical ensemble. Larger cooperative energies, in particular those predicted by the grand canonical ensemble, lead to instabilities (cascade processes) in oxygen release within the canonical approach. Oxygen-binding fluctuations within this approach are sizably smaller than those in the grand canonical situation. These results suggest that the hopping diffusion of oxygen from one hemoglobin to another may play a role in oxygen diffusion within the RBC.

papers.title: Spontaneous Mutations from Terahertz Proton Tunneling
papers.abstract: Protons in the bonds between base pairs of the double helix store the code of life by breaking the dyad symmetry that swaps the sense strand with its complementary partner. When these bonds break during replication and transcription, pairs of protons switch sides, restoring dyad symmetry and destroying genetic information. The observed rate of such spontaneous mutations is obtained in the sudden approximation for bond breaking provided protons in bonds between bases tunnel across the gap with terahertz frequency.

papers.title: Automatic Generation of Novel Highly-Functional Molecular Sequences
papers.abstract: While multiple methods now exist to generate functional sequence variants from existing annotated examples, it is unclear how well such methods can be used to generate sequences that exceed the functionality of those contained in the example set. Using two complete fitness landscapes, we quantify how effectively generative tools can search sequence space and find rare, novel, highly functional sequences, focusing on variational auto-encoders and information-theoretic methods. We find that an information-theoretic method that does not require training and runs significantly faster than standard Machine-Learning/Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) methods also is significantly more effective in finding rare highly-functional sequences. We discuss the application of this novel method to discover rare polypeptides with anti-bacterial properties that are specific to bacterial, but not eukaryotic, cell membranes.
